extracted.intended_audience: engineers and informed readers interested in 19th-century bridge and railway engineering
extracted.subtask_short: bridge design evaluation for long spans
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and comparative guidance for selecting and designing long-span railway bridges (tubular, lattice, trellis, suspension, iron-arch) with special attention to rigidity, strength, economy, permanence, and resistance to ice and derailment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall selection criteria for bridge type
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen design must be unimpeachable as respects strength, efficiency, economy, and permanency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Stephenson vindicated the tubular plan to the directors by proving it appropriate in strength, efficiency, economy and with view to permanency. Various methods (suspension, iron arches, horizontal girders) were considered and weighed against these four core requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsuitability of suspension bridges for heavy railway traffic
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension bridges are defective in rigidity, limiting speed and weight of trains and thus traffic capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of defective rigidity a long suspension bridge would allow only about 20 trains per 24 hours on the Victoria Bridge length — insufficient for anticipated traffic. Adding material to increase rigidity approximates a beam and negates the cost advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsuitability of iron-arch bridges where large headway for ice is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Iron-arch designs may be inapplicable when large headway is needed for ice passage, because arches' springings must be clear of the water-line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To provide the necessary ice headway an iron-arched bridge would require raising the entire road and considerably increasing upper-work expenditure, making it impractical for the St. Lawrence crossing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruling principle in calculating girder strength (top and bottom members)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimate strength primarily resides in the top (compression) and bottom (tension) members; for equal span and depth the effective material in these members must be the same across girder types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Stephenson: 'Primarily and essentially, the ultimate strength is considered to exist in the top and bottom... therefore, whatever be the class of girders, they must all be alike in amount of effective material in these members, if their spans and depths are the same, and they have to sustain the same amount of load.' The comparative merit reduces to the method of connecting the top and bottom webs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the method of connecting top and bottom webs
rubrics_metrics.description: The way the top and bottom webs are connected (continuous boiler plates vs. flat bars forming struts/ties) determines rigidity, effective strength, and practical economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tubular connection uses continuous riveted boiler plates; lattice/trellis use numerous flat bars. Advocates of bars cite material saving; Stephenson argued boiler-plate sides equal or superior in effective strength and rigidity, with examples showing comparable or favourable material weight for tubes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative rigidity and deflection under passing load (tubular advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tubular girders exhibit superior rigidity and smaller deflection under passing trains compared to lattice/trellis girders of similar span and dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical comparisons: lattice girder over the Trent (span 240.5 ft, width 13 ft) weighed 292 tons; Victoria tube (span 242 ft, width 16 ft) weighed 275 tons. Travelers note greater deflection on lattice bridges; Stephenson asserted tubes are decidedly superior in rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material economy trade-off: bars versus plates
rubrics_metrics.description: Lattice/trellis claim material savings by using bars; tubular claims show that boiler-plate sides can be equal in economy while providing greater rigidity and effective strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephenson contrasted actual weights of comparable spans to show the tube could be lighter or comparable in weight while being stiffer. He also argued that the sides of lattice/trellis serve merely to connect top and bottom and add to strain on those members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety in derailment: structural robustness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Bridges must be safe in the event of a train running off the line; tubular bridges are preferable as they can often survive such accidents whereas trellis/lattice bridges are likely to be destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephenson emphasized that on long bridges (e.g., mile-plus) the contingency of a train running off the line was highly significant in the directors' decision for the tubular design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation design for piers exposed to heavy ice forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations must be placed in solid rock and piers must be massive to resist prodigious ice forces; timber cribwork, piling, or rubble foundations are inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ice from thousands of square miles of lakes piles up (40–50 ft) and exerts overwhelming pressure, the Victoria Bridge piers were founded in solid rock and built massive (centre piers 18 ft wide, others 15 ft) with thousands of tons of masonry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of ice-breakers/cutwaters on piers
rubrics_metrics.description: Piers should have an inclined plane of great stone blocks on the up-river side to arrest and break ice; blocks of 7–10 tons clamped with iron rivets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To arrest and break the ice an inclined face composed of large stone blocks was added to each pier; this measure was critical to resist the immense ice-jam forces observed during construction (March–April 1858), when piers largely escaped uninjured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Massive masonry piers and weight considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Piers must contain very large quantities of solid masonry (several thousand tons per pier) to withstand ice and hydraulic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Victoria Bridge piers contained some six to ten thousand tons of solid masonry each; such mass was necessary given the avalanching ice and high currents of the St. Lawrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary works vulnerability during ice events
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary timber cribwork and floating pontoons used during construction are vulnerable to severe ice movement and can be considerably damaged even when permanent piers resist the forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the 1858 ice movement the 'cribwork' erected to facilitate pontoons was considerably disturbed and in places seriously damaged, illustrating that temporary methods may fail under extreme seasonal forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of roadway relative to tubes (inside vs upon)
rubrics_metrics.description: The roadway may be carried within the tube (where span large) or upon the tubes (modified form as on Nile bridges); selection depends on span, local conditions, and erection considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tubular bridges at Menai and Conway carried the road within the tube; on the Nile Robert Stephenson applied a modified form where the road was carried upon the tubes. Erection was executed with workmen and plant sent from England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of trellis/warren (triangular) girders for certain contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Trellis (Warren) girders provide triangulation, comparative rigidity, strength, lightness, and economy, making them suitable for long Indian rivers and viaducts like the Crumlin viaduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trellis/triangular girders are widely used where easy transport and erection are priorities; the Crumlin viaduct (200 ft high) is cited as an excellent specimen entitled to be regarded as a remarkable engineering work.
